newsitem.title: USA: House passes disaster aid bill, faces White House veto.
newsitem.headline: House passes disaster aid bill, faces White House veto.

text.p: The House Thursday passed an emergency spending bill providing $8.4 billion to aid weather-ravaged states and fund U.S. military operations overseas, despite a veto threat from President Clinton.
Intended as a lifeboat for flood-weary regions, the measure is looking more like a sinking ship weighed down by contentious spending provisions unrelated to disaster aid.
After heavy lobbying from Republican leaders, the House voted 227-197 to continue federal programs automatically at current levels next year if spending bills are not approved.
Clinton has threatened to veto the bill if it arrives on his desk with the spending measure attached.

The White House charges the plan takes the pressure off Congress to make tough spendings decisions, while providing far less for domestic programs than Clinton was promised under a balanced budget deal.
"This is like using a sledgehammer to kill an ant," said Wisconsin Democratic Rep. David Obey.

Spending disputes forced two unpopular government shutdowns in fiscal 1996, which the public blamed on Republicans. House leaders call the autopilot proposal an insurance policy to prevent closures and protect taxpayers.
"Many of us are saying we do not want to use any threat of shutting the government down. Now we hear (Democrats) saying 'you've got to do it,'" complained Oklahoma Republican Rep. Ernest Istook.

The legislation, passed 244-178, provides $5.5 billion in disaster aid to more than 30 states. It also includes nearly $2 billion to fund American peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and U.S. military flights in the Gulf.
Clinton has threatened to veto the Senate-passed version of the bill, also due to the automatic spending proposal.

In a move applauded by the administration the House voted to increase funding for a nutrition aid for poor women and children. Administration officials had warned nearly 200,000 needy children could lose aid without the extra funds.

The bill originally provided only half of the $76 million requested by the White House for the Women, Infants and Children program. Under attack from Democrats, the House passed a bipartisan amendment granting the full amount.
"This should not be a partisan issue ... this is about taking food out of the mouths of little babies," said New Jersey Republican Rep. Marge Roukema.
But 89 Republicans voted no, saying there was more than enough money in the pipeline to support all participants now in the program. No Democrats voted against the amendment.

"The ugliness of demagoguery and grandstanding have crept into the WIC program," said New Mexico Republican Joe Skeen. "In a very concerted political move to show who loves children we have state WIC directors telling misleading stories."

The House also extended federal disability aid to legal immigrants through September. An estimated 500,000 aliens were slated to lose disability benefits by Aug. 22 under a welfare law. A recent balanced budget agreement, if approved by Congress, continues aid to most of those recipients.
"The message that we are sending out about this country is that we are mean-spirited and racist, is that the kind of message we want?" said Corrine Brown, a Florida Democrat.
Lawmakers engaged in a regional fight over a provision of the bill opening what had been a sole-source contract to supply paper for U.S. currency.
The Crane and Co. firm of Massachusetts has provided currency paper for decades, protected by a law requiring paper to be made in America by firms 90 percent U.S.-owned.

The bill would open bidding for the $75 million contract to firms 50 percent U.S.-owned. A Crown Vantage plant in New Jersey wants to bid for the work with a subsidiary of the British-based Thomas DeLaRue company.
Lawmakers blocked the bill Wednesday in part because the currency amendment was to be deleted. Thursday it stayed in.
